new_entities.name: Body recomposition and weight loss
new_entities.description: Intentional reduction of body weight and fat mass through caloric restriction or bariatric weight-loss strategies.

new_entities.name: Testosterone in obese men
new_entities.description: Changes in testosterone concentrations among men with obesity.

edges.effect_quant: A 2019 meta-analysis of bariatric surgery studies involving 1,022 men found significant post-weight-loss increases in both free and calculated testosterone, and a smaller dietary study doubled mean total testosterone from 6.97 to 13.21 nmol/L after 12 weeks of caloric restriction.
edges.population: adult men with obesity, including men with obesity-related hypogonadism and men undergoing bariatric surgery or intensive caloric restriction
edges.mechanism: Losing fat mass reduces aromatase-driven conversion of testosterone to estradiol and can improve insulin resistance and hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal signaling. That makes the endocrine benefit of weight loss more pathophysiologic than supplement-like: it removes a driver of suppression rather than forcing testosterone upward directly.
edges.summary: Weight loss is one of the more believable non-drug ways to improve testosterone in obese men. The evidence is not just associative: both caloric restriction and bariatric surgery studies show that substantial fat loss often lifts testosterone, particularly when obesity-related hypogonadism is present.
edges.caveats: Not every man normalizes testosterone with weight loss, and the biggest hormonal gains tend to come with large or sustained weight reduction. This edge is strongest for men with genuine obesity-related suppression, not for already-lean men chasing marginal optimization.

evidence.citation: Lee Y et al 2019 Obes Surg
evidence.notes: Impact of Bariatric Surgery on Male Sex Hormones and Sperm Quality: a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
